preamble: Raising of unstressed [e] to the near-close [ɪ], merging it with unstressed /i/. In standard Russian this merger is called ikanye: after palatalized (soft) consonants and /j/, unstressed /e/ is pronounced like unstressed /i/, as [ɪ]. Thus леса 'forests' [lʲɪˈsa] (cf. лес [lʲes] 'forest') sounds the same as лиса 'vixen', and черепа 'skulls' [t͡ɕɪrʲɪˈpa] contrasts with stressed череп [ˈt͡ɕerʲɪp] 'skull'. Yanushevskaya & Bunčić (2015) define ikan'e as the merger of unstressed /e/ and /i/ after palatalized consonants, and their St Petersburg speaker has it. The Old Petersburgian pronunciation and some rural dialects kept the two apart before the stress, with леса as [lʲɘˈsa].

examples.note: Homophonous with лиса [lʲɪˈsa] 'vixen'. The Old Petersburgian pronunciation kept [lʲɘˈsa].

Yanushevskaya & Bunčić (2015), describing a St Petersburg speaker, transcribe the same [ɪ]: решили [rʲɪˈʃɨⁱˑlʲɪ] 'decided', петербургский [pʲɪtʲɪrˈbuˑrskʲɪi̯] 'of St Petersburg' (retraction diacritics omitted).
